segments.say: Let's talk about rewards now. Not the rewards inside the brain, but the ones out in the world, and the surprising ways their timing shapes what we do. Our story starts in New York, in the 1890s, with a young scientist and a group of hungry cats.

In 1898, Edward Thorndike, then a graduate student at Columbia University, built a set of wooden puzzle boxes. A cat placed inside could get out, and reach a little food, by pulling a loop of string, or pressing a lever, or stepping on a small platform. Thorndike timed each escape, over and over.

show.what: Placed cats in puzzle boxes that opened when they pulled a loop or pressed a lever, and timed how quickly they escaped over many trials

segments.say: What he found was not a flash of understanding. The cats didn't seem to suddenly realise how the box worked. Instead, they scrambled about, hit the right move by chance, and escaped. And on later tries, they got there a little faster, then a little faster again. The useless movements slowly dropped away.

Thorndike summed it up in what he called the law of effect. Actions that are followed by a satisfying result tend to be repeated. Actions followed by discomfort tend to fade. It sounds almost too obvious to say. But it became one of the foundations of the science of learning.

show.what: Actions followed by a satisfying result become more likely; actions followed by discomfort become less likely

segments.say: Decades later, the American psychologist B. F. Skinner took that idea and made it precise. He built a small chamber where a rat could press a lever, or a pigeon could peck a little key, and food would sometimes drop into a tray. A pen recorded every single response, minute by minute.

show.what: Built a small chamber where an animal could press a lever or peck a key for food, and recorded every response over time

segments.say: And here's where it gets interesting. Skinner didn't have to give food after every press. He could give it after every tenth press. Or after the first press once a minute had passed. Or at random, sometimes after two presses, sometimes after twenty. These patterns are called schedules of reinforcement.

In 1957, Charles Ferster and Skinner published a huge book, Schedules of Reinforcement, full of records from pigeons. It showed that each kind of schedule produces its own reliable pattern of behaviour. Change the schedule, and you change the pattern, almost like changing the rhythm of a song.

show.what: Showed in great detail that different reward schedules produce very different, very reliable patterns of responding

segments.say: Here are a few of those patterns, simplified. A reward every time gives steady behaviour, which stops quickly when the rewards end. Rewards at fixed times give a pause after each one, then a rush as the next one nears. Rewards after an unpredictable number of tries give fast, steady responding. And unpredictable rewards tend to keep behaviour going longest after they stop.

show.title: A few patterns
items: Every time: steady, but stops quickly
At fixed times: a pause, then a rush
After an unpredictable number: fast and steady

segments.say: Think about why that might be. If a reward always comes after one press, you notice straight away when it stops. But if rewards have always been unpredictable, a long dry spell doesn't feel like the end. The next try might be the one. Maybe this time.

Many researchers have pointed out how much this resembles some modern habits. Pulling down to refresh a feed. Checking for messages. Most of the time there's nothing new. Every so often, there's something lovely. It's a pattern that can keep the hand moving, even when the eyes are tired.

A word of care, though. People are not pigeons in a box. We have plans, memories, values and other people around us, and we can notice what we're doing. The schedules are a powerful influence on behaviour, not a complete explanation of it. Still, knowing the pattern can make it a little easier to see.

In 1948, Skinner tried something curious. He gave hungry pigeons a little food at regular intervals, no matter what they were doing. Nothing they did made any difference. And yet many of the birds developed strange rituals. One turned in circles. Another kept thrusting its head into an upper corner of the cage.

show.what: Gave hungry pigeons food at regular intervals no matter what they did, and many developed odd repeated rituals

segments.say: Skinner called this superstition. Whatever the bird happened to be doing when the food arrived seemed to get stamped in, and repeated, and so it was more likely to be doing it when the next food came along. A coincidence turned into a habit. It's easy to think of human lucky rituals that might work in a similar way.
There's another old finding about rewards that's worth meeting, because it shows up in rats, and also, rather charmingly, in coffee shops.

In 1932, Clark Hull, whom we met earlier, described what he called the goal gradient. The idea was that the closer an animal is to a reward, the harder it works. Rats running down a straight alley towards food tended to run faster as they neared the end.

show.what: Proposed the goal gradient: animals speed up as they get closer to a reward, with rats running faster near the end of a runway

segments.say: You've probably felt this yourself. The last few pages of a good book go faster than the first few. The final stretch of a long walk home has its own extra energy. When the end is in sight, something seems to switch on.

In 2006, Ran Kivetz, Oleg Urminsky and Yuhuang Zheng, at Columbia University, looked for the goal gradient in people. They studied a café reward card, where each coffee earned a stamp, and a full card earned a free coffee. And they found that people came back more often, with shorter gaps between visits, as their card filled up.

show.who: Ran Kivetz, Oleg Urminsky & Yuhuang Zheng
show.what: Studied café reward cards and found that people visited more often as they got closer to a free coffee

segments.say: Then they tried a clever twist. Some customers received a card that needed ten stamps. Others received a card that needed twelve stamps, but already had two stamped as a bonus. Both groups had exactly ten more coffees to go. The only difference was how the card looked.

And yet the head-start card was filled faster, on average. Feeling that you've already begun, even when the start was given to you, seemed to pull people along. Progress, or even the look of progress, is motivating in itself.

One way to understand this is that the remaining distance feels smaller when you think of yourself as partway there. Ten steps out of ten feels like a beginning. Ten steps out of twelve feels like you're well on your way. We'll come back to this idea of progress later tonight.
Picture a coffee cup on a small café table, and a little card beside it. A few marks already on it. That small sense of being partway there is enough to change what people do.

So rewards shape behaviour powerfully. Their timing, their predictability, and how close they seem all matter. It might seem, then, that the simplest way to motivate anyone is just to add more rewards. More stamps. More prizes. More praise.

Many people use this quite naturally. A cup of tea after finishing a chore. A short walk after a long stretch of work. A chapter of a book once the dishes are done. These small rewards, close in time to the effort, follow exactly the kind of pattern Thorndike saw in his cats.

So that's our third stop. Satisfying results tend to get repeated. The schedule of rewards shapes the pattern of behaviour. Unpredictable rewards keep us going longest. And we speed up as the goal comes into view.

show.title: The third stop
items: We speed up near the goal

segments.say: But rewards are only part of the picture. Before we come back to the puzzle of the child and the drawings, let's ask a bigger question. Beyond food and warmth, what do people actually need? One famous answer is a pyramid. And the story behind it is not quite what you've been told.
